from fractions import Fraction as Q

def eta(a,b):
 if b<a: return 1-b/a
 if b>a: return 1-(1-b)/(1-a)
 return Q(0)

# Two equally weighted groups with label prevalence epsilon and FNRs 1/4 and 1/2.
# All negative examples are classified correctly in both groups.
prevalence=Q(1,10000)
rates=[Q(1,4),Q(1,2)]
candidates=[Q(0),Q(1),*rates]
unfairness=min(sum(prevalence*Q(1,2)*eta(a,b) for b in rates) for a in candidates)
print('Rare-disease example:', {'prevalence':float(prevalence), 'FNRs':[float(x) for x in rates], 'unfairness':float(unfairness), 'unfairness/prevalence':str(unfairness/prevalence)})

# A perfect fair binary classifier has zero discrepancy by Eq. (17),
# but the binary expression after Eq. (20) assigns accuracy as the error term.

pi=[Q(1,2),Q(1,2)]
false_rates=[Q(0),Q(0)]
binary_written=sum(pi[y]*(beta*eta(false_rates[y],false_rates[y])+(1-beta)*(1-false_rates[y])) for y in range(2))
print('Perfect classifier discrepancy:', {'Eq17':0,'Section7.1_written_value':float(binary_written)})

strengths: The paper addresses an important auditing problem: inferring classifier properties when only group-level label proportions are available. Optimizing over confusion matrices consistent with these proportions provides a useful framework for determining what the available information can establish.

The mixture-based unfairness measure has a precise mathematical definition and a useful monotonicity property under merging predicted labels. The binary candidate-set reductions and the constructive multiclass bounding procedures provide substantive technical content.

The experiments cover hundreds of Census classification problems, Natality data, and several aggregate-data applications. Comparisons with individual-level evaluation and ablations of greedy initialization and local refinement are valuable. Several multiclass bounds coincide, and the manuscript supplies pseudocode, proofs, and a code link.
weaknesses: Major objective inconsistencies affect reproducibility of the main results. Section 7.1 applies τβ(a,b)=βη(a,b)+(1−β)(1−b) to false-positive and false-negative rates, so its error component becomes accuracy, contrary to Eq. (17) and Algorithm 2, line 8. Separately, Eqs. (26) and (29) omit the population weights w_gπ_g^y from the error term: F^y is defined using unweighted indicators. These may be transcription errors, but corrected derivations and confirmation of which objective generated the experiments are necessary.

Lemma 7.3 does not establish the advertised numerical tolerance. Its proof bounds the derivative of η while omitting the linear error component of τβ. For example, a=b=1/2, c=d=1/4, and β=1/2 give ψ(x)=5/8−x/8 on (0,1), whereas the stated derivative bound is zero. Consequently, Algorithm 2's accuracy guarantee requires repair. Moreover, its approximate value V must be reduced by the certified tolerance before being used as a rigorous lower bound.

The claimed behavior under class imbalance in Section 5.2 is incorrect. With two equally weighted groups, disease prevalence p in each, identical false-positive rates, and false-negative rates 1/4 and 1/2, the proposed unfairness is p/6 and vanishes as the disease becomes rare. More generally, choosing the identity confusion matrix as the baseline proves unfairness ≤ error. The measure remains meaningful as a population-weighted quantity, but its asserted sensitivity to rare-disease disparities requires qualification.

Section 7 asserts that sweeping the weighted discrepancy objective solves error minimization under an arbitrary unfairness budget. Such an equivalence requires justification for this nonconvex problem: weighted sums generally recover only supported Pareto points. Without an additional result, the experiments do not establish complete, best-possible fairness–error frontiers.

The multiclass aggregate-data evaluation reports only local upper bounds on minimal unfairness at β=1, without corresponding lower bounds or evaluation of the general discrepancy tradeoff. Their tightness is therefore unknown. Table 5 includes an upper bound of 3.20% when actual unfairness is 0.77%, demonstrating a substantial optimization gap. Trends in the election upper bounds, or similar education upper bounds, cannot establish corresponding trends or similarities in actual unfairness.

The applications need stronger treatment of population mismatch and uncertainty. General-population cancer incidence is used as the true-label proportion for Bing users without establishing that these quantities match. Section 4 briefly suggests interval constraints, but comparable uncertainty analysis is absent from the main procedures and case studies. Clipping probabilities and modifying prediction proportions also change the optimization inputs without certifying bounds for the original inputs. These issues limit the population-level conclusions.

Incremental originality is insufficiently delineated. The manuscript acknowledges that it extends Sabato and Yom-Tov (ICML 2020), but does not clearly identify which definitions, binary results, algorithms, and experiments are inherited. A direct account of the new contributions is needed to assess significance relative to this particularly close predecessor.
